author: volatility
note: Predicates 57-60. LOW/HIGH_VOLATILITY compare the reference bar range r0 against QM_PP_Atr(b,1,10). The group default_filler_series is a single uniform bar [100.0,100.5,99.5,100.0] with range exactly 1.0 and close 100.0; cycled to fill indices 1..11 it makes atr10 = 1.0 exactly (for every i in 1..10, close[i+1]=100.0 lies inside [99.5,100.5] so TR = high-low = 1.0, and the 10-term mean is 1.0). LOW/HIGH fixtures therefore supply only bars[0] (the bar under test) and let the filler set a known ATR baseline of 1.0. VOL_CONTRACTION/VOL_EXPANSION read only bars 0,1,2 (required=3) so they supply all three bars explicitly and the filler is never used. All bars centered on 100.0 with open=close=100.0 so body=0 and range=high-low; high=100+R/2, low=100-R/2.

fixtures.rationale: Low volatility means the just-closed bar's range is far smaller than the recent average range. The filler pins the 10-bar ATR at 1.0; this reference bar spans only 0.30, less than a third of the average, an unmistakably quiet bar.
A bar spanning 2.00 against a recent average range of 1.00 is twice as wide as normal: the very opposite of low volatility. This attacks the r0<0.7*atr10 clause with a large reference range.

A reference bar whose range 1.00 equals the recent average range 1.00 is an ordinary bar, not a compressed one. Volatility that matches the baseline is not low volatility. Also attacks the r0<0.7*atr10 clause but from the average-range side rather than the wide side.

The ten prior bars are perfectly flat (zero range each), so there is no historical volatility baseline against which to call this bar quiet. With atr10=0 the predicate cannot assert low volatility. This attacks the atr10>0 guard, a different clause than the range comparison.

atr10=1.0 so the threshold is 0.7*1.0=0.70. Reference range 0.65 sits below the ceiling by 0.05 (~7%), inside the low-volatility region, so r0<0.7*atr10 holds and the predicate fires. Not placed on 0.70 to avoid float-equality ambiguity.

Same atr10=1.0 baseline, threshold 0.70. Reference range 0.75 sits above the ceiling by 0.05 (~7%), outside the low-volatility region, so r0<0.7*atr10 is false. Only bars[0]'s range changed from the inside case, isolating this single clause.

High volatility means the just-closed bar's range is much larger than the recent average. The filler pins atr10 at 1.0; this reference bar spans 2.50, two and a half times the average, an unmistakably violent bar.
A bar spanning only 0.50 against a recent average range of 1.00 is half as wide as normal: a quiet bar, the opposite of high volatility. Attacks the r0>1.3*atr10 clause with a small reference range.

A reference bar whose range 1.00 equals the recent average range 1.00 is an ordinary bar. Volatility at the baseline is not high volatility. Attacks the r0>1.3*atr10 clause from the average-range side rather than the calm side.

The ten prior bars are perfectly flat (zero range each) so atr10=0. Even though this reference bar spans a huge 5.00, there is no historical baseline to declare it a volatility expansion; a single wide bar after a dead-flat history is undefined, not high volatility. Attacks the atr10>0 guard, a different clause.

atr10=1.0 so the threshold is 1.3*1.0=1.30. Reference range 1.40 sits above the floor by 0.10 (~7.7%), inside the high-volatility region, so r0>1.3*atr10 holds. Kept off 1.30 to avoid float-equality ambiguity.

Same atr10=1.0 baseline, threshold 1.30. Reference range 1.20 sits below the floor by 0.10 (~7.7%), outside the high-volatility region, so r0>1.3*atr10 is false. Only bars[0]'s range changed from the inside case, isolating this clause.

Volatility contraction is successively narrowing bars as time advances. Oldest bar (index 2) range 3.00, middle (index 1) range 2.00, newest (index 0) range 1.00: a clean monotone squeeze, so r0<range1 (1<2) and range1<range2 (2<3) both hold.

The two older bars narrow (index 2 range 3.00, index 1 range 2.00) but the newest bar (index 0) blows out to range 2.50, wider than its predecessor. A squeeze that reverses on the last bar is not a contraction. Attacks the r0<range1 clause (2.5<2.0 is false).

Newest bar narrows (index 0 range 1.00 < index 1 range 2.00) but the middle bar is wider than the oldest (index 1 range 2.00 > index 2 range 1.50), so the range sequence is not monotonically shrinking. Attacks the range1<range2 clause (2.0<1.5 is false).

Isolating the r0<range1 comparison with range1<range2 held comfortably true (1.00<2.00). Reference range 0.90 is below range1 1.00 by 0.10 (~10%), inside, so the strict r0<range1 holds and the predicate fires. Not placed at equality since r0<range1 is a strict comparison.

Same setup with range1<range2 held true, but reference range 1.10 is above range1 1.00 by 0.10 (~10%), outside, so r0<range1 is false. Only bars[0] changed from the inside case, isolating this comparison.

Isolating the range1<range2 comparison with r0<range1 held comfortably true (0.50<1.00). Middle range1 1.00 is below oldest range2 1.10 by 0.10 (~10%), inside, so the strict range1<range2 holds and the predicate fires.

Same setup with r0<range1 held true, but middle range1 1.00 is above oldest range2 0.90 by 0.10 (~10%), outside, so range1<range2 is false. Only bars[2] changed from the inside case, isolating this comparison.

Volatility expansion is successively widening bars as time advances. Oldest bar (index 2) range 1.00, middle (index 1) range 2.00, newest (index 0) range 3.00: a clean monotone broadening, so r0>range1 (3>2) and range1>range2 (2>1) both hold.

The two older bars widen (index 2 range 1.00, index 1 range 2.00) but the newest bar (index 0) contracts to range 1.50, narrower than its predecessor. A broadening that reverses on the last bar is not an expansion. Attacks the r0>range1 clause (1.5>2.0 is false).

Newest bar widens (index 0 range 3.00 > index 1 range 2.00) but the middle bar is narrower than the oldest (index 1 range 2.00 < index 2 range 2.50), so the range sequence is not monotonically growing. Attacks the range1>range2 clause (2.0>2.5 is false).

Isolating the r0>range1 comparison with range1>range2 held comfortably true (1.00>0.50). Reference range 1.10 is above range1 1.00 by 0.10 (~10%), inside, so the strict r0>range1 holds and the predicate fires. Kept off equality since the comparison is strict.

Same setup with range1>range2 held true, but reference range 0.90 is below range1 1.00 by 0.10 (~10%), outside, so r0>range1 is false. Only bars[0] changed from the inside case, isolating this comparison.

Isolating the range1>range2 comparison with r0>range1 held comfortably true (2.00>1.10). Middle range1 1.10 is above oldest range2 1.00 by 0.10 (~10%), inside, so the strict range1>range2 holds and the predicate fires.

Same setup with r0>range1 held true, but middle range1 0.90 is below oldest range2 1.00 by 0.10 (~10%), outside, so range1>range2 is false. Only bars[1] changed from the inside case, isolating this comparison.
